options.label: A shrub or tree that grows mainly in coastal saline or brackish water
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves are woody plants that live in salty or brackish coastal water.

options.label: A type of seaweed that floats in the open ocean
options.feedback: Incorrect. Seaweed is an alga, not a shrub or tree, and mangroves grow rooted in coastal shallows, not floating in open water.

options.label: A freshwater plant that lives only in deep lakes
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves need saline or brackish water; they do not grow in deep freshwater lakes.

options.label: A grass that grows in dry inland deserts
options.feedback: Incorrect. A mangrove is a woody shrub or tree, and it lives in wet coastal conditions, not dry deserts.

items.ok_line: A mangrove is a salt-tolerant shrub or tree of coastal waters.
items.ko_line: The other choices describe different kinds of plants or habitats.
items.exp_text: A mangrove is a shrub or tree that grows mainly in coastal saline or brackish water. It lives where most plants cannot survive, because it is specially adapted to salty, waterlogged conditions.

items.prompt: Where in the world do mangroves mainly grow?

options.label: Only in the coldest polar oceans
options.feedback: Incorrect. Polar seas are far too cold for mangroves, which need warm tropical and subtropical waters.

options.label: In tropical and subtropical coastal areas, mainly between latitudes 30° N and 30° S
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves occur worldwide in these warm bands, with the largest area within 5° of the equator.

options.label: Inland on high mountain slopes
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves are coastal plants; they do not grow on mountains.

options.label: In deep ocean water far from any shore
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves need to root in coastal sediments, not float in the open sea.

items.ok_line: Mangroves grow in warm coastal regions near the equator.
items.ko_line: The correct habitat is tropical and subtropical coasts.
items.exp_text: Mangroves occur worldwide in tropical and subtropical coastal areas, mainly between latitudes 30° N and 30° S. Most of the world's mangroves lie within 5° of the equator, where the climate is warm and wet.

items.prompt: What kind of water can mangroves tolerate?

options.label: Only completely fresh water
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves are salt-tolerant; they live in saline or brackish water, not only fresh water.

options.label: Only boiling hot water
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves live in normal-temperature coastal waters, not boiling water.

options.label: Brackish water, pure seawater, and water up to twice as salty as the ocean
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves can handle from brackish water through seawater to very salty water concentrated by evaporation.

options.label: Only water with no salt at all
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves need some salt and can tolerate high salinity; they are not plants of salt-free water.

items.ok_line: Mangroves survive brackish, seawater, and even saltier conditions.
items.ko_line: The correct range includes brackish and very salty water.
items.exp_text: Mangroves are halophytic and salt-tolerant. They can grow in brackish water, in pure seawater with 3 to 4% salinity, and even in water concentrated by evaporation to over twice that, up to 9% salinity.

items.prompt: What are the root-like structures called pneumatophores used for?

options.label: To anchor the tree in deep ocean sand
options.feedback: Incorrect. Pneumatophores stick up out of the soil, not down into it; anchoring is done by other roots.

options.label: To catch small fish for food
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves are plants; their roots do not catch animals.

options.label: To store fresh water for dry seasons
options.feedback: Incorrect. Pneumatophores are breathing tubes that absorb gases; they do not store water.

options.label: To absorb oxygen from the air above the waterlogged soil
options.feedback: Correct. Pneumatophores stick up like straws and let the roots breathe air.

items.ok_line: Pneumatophores bring oxygen to roots in waterlogged mud.
items.ko_line: These structures are for gas exchange, not anchoring, feeding, or storing water.
items.exp_text: Pneumatophores are specialized root-like structures that stick up out of the waterlogged soil. They allow the mangrove to absorb oxygen directly from the atmosphere, since the mud itself has very little oxygen.

items.prompt: How does the red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) keep itself above the water in the most flooded areas?

options.label: It props itself up with stilt or prop roots and breathes through lenticels in its bark
options.feedback: Correct. The red mangrove uses prop roots to rise above the water and lenticels to take in air.

options.label: It floats on large air-filled leaves
options.feedback: Incorrect. The red mangrove does not float; it is rooted and uses prop roots, not leaves, for support.

options.label: It grows a thick trunk that pushes it out of the water entirely
options.feedback: Incorrect. The red mangrove does not lift itself out of water with its trunk; stilt roots do the job.

options.label: It bends over and lets the tide carry it
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves are fixed in place; they do not drift with tides.

items.ok_line: Stilt roots raise the red mangrove above the water.
items.ko_line: It is the prop roots, not leaves or floating, that keep it upright.
items.exp_text: In the most inundated places, the red mangrove props itself above the water level with stilt or prop roots. It absorbs air through lenticels in its bark, which are tiny pores that let gases pass.

items.prompt: Why do mangroves grow in the upper half of the intertidal zone?

options.label: Because they need dry land all the time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves must be flooded by tides; they do not live on permanently dry land.

options.label: Because they cannot survive any salt at all
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves are salt-tolerant, so salt is not a reason to avoid the intertidal zone.

options.label: Because there they cope best with the low-oxygen, salty conditions
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves are adapted to the harsh conditions of the upper intertidal zone.

options.label: Because they only grow where there is no water
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves need regular tidal water; they do not live where water never reaches.

items.ok_line: Mangroves thrive in the upper intertidal zone.
items.ko_line: They live near the tide line, not on dry land or away from water.
items.exp_text: Mangroves are adapted to the low-oxygen conditions of waterlogged mud, but they are most likely to thrive in the upper half of the intertidal zone. That is the area that is flooded by high tides but exposed at low tide, where conditions suit them best.

items.prompt: What does a mangrove's 'sacrificial leaf' do?

options.label: It collects food for the whole tree
options.feedback: Incorrect. The sacrificial leaf is about removing salt, not gathering food.

options.label: It blocks sunlight from reaching other leaves
options.feedback: Incorrect. The leaf does not block light; it is shed after concentrating salt.

options.label: It repairs damage to the roots
options.feedback: Incorrect. The sacrificial leaf has nothing to do with root repair.

options.label: It absorbs salt, then the plant sheds it to get rid of the salt
options.feedback: Correct. This leaf concentrates salt and is dropped to remove the salt from the plant.

items.ok_line: Old leaves carry away salt when they fall.
items.ko_line: The sacrificial leaf's purpose is salt removal, not nutrition or shading.
items.exp_text: In the sacrificial leaf idea, salt that builds up in a mangrove's shoots concentrates in old leaves. The plant then sheds those leaves, carrying the salt away with them. Recent research on the red mangrove, though, found that older yellowing leaves do not actually have more salt than greener ones.

items.prompt: Why is the soil in a mangrove swamp low in oxygen?

options.label: Because the trees use up all the oxygen at night
options.feedback: Incorrect. The low oxygen is due to the soil being constantly waterlogged, not to the trees' respiration.

options.label: Because the soil is perpetually waterlogged
options.feedback: Correct. Waterlogged mud has little free oxygen available for roots.

options.label: Because the soil is made of pure sand
options.feedback: Incorrect. The soil is fine sediment with high organic content, and sand does not explain the low oxygen.

options.label: Because the trees release methane that displaces oxygen
options.feedback: Incorrect. Anaerobic bacteria release methane in the soil, but they are a consequence of the waterlogging, not the cause of low oxygen.

items.ok_line: Constant waterlogging leaves little air in the soil.
items.ko_line: Permanent water is what deprives the soil of oxygen.
items.exp_text: Because the soil is perpetually waterlogged, little free oxygen is available. Water fills the spaces between sediment grains, so air cannot reach the roots. That is why mangroves need special roots to breathe.

items.prompt: What do mangrove roots do with gases when they are submerged during high tide?

options.label: They store gases inside the roots and process them even while underwater
options.feedback: Correct. Mangroves keep gases in their roots and use them even when the tide covers them.

options.label: They release all gases into the water immediately
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves hold and process gases; they do not simply let them go into the water.

options.label: They stop breathing until the tide goes out
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves continue to process stored gases, so they do not stop.

options.label: They turn gases into liquid inside the roots
options.feedback: Incorrect. Gases are stored as gases, not turned into liquid.

items.ok_line: Roots hold gases and keep working underwater.
items.ko_line: Mangroves store gases rather than releasing or stopping.
items.exp_text: Mangroves store gases directly inside their roots and process them even when the roots are submerged during high tide. This lets them keep taking in what they need despite the water covering their breathing structures.

items.prompt: How do mangroves limit the water they lose through their leaves?

options.label: They grow no leaves at all
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves have leaves; they just control water loss through them.

options.label: They close their roots completely
options.feedback: Incorrect. Limiting water loss happens in the leaves, not by closing roots.

options.label: They restrict the opening of their stomata and change leaf orientation
options.feedback: Correct. Closing stomata and turning leaves away from the midday sun reduce evaporation.

options.label: They store all water in their trunks
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mangroves reduce leaf water loss rather than storing water in trunks.

items.ok_line: Stomata and leaf angles cut water loss.
items.ko_line: It is the stomata and leaf position, not leaves or roots, that help.
items.exp_text: Because fresh water is scarce in salty soils, mangroves limit water loss from their leaves. They can restrict the opening of their stomata, the pores that exchange gases, and they also vary leaf orientation to avoid the harsh midday sun, reducing evaporation.
